title: Inter-process Communication
body:
The two forms of Inter-Process communication are [[Shared Memory]] and [[Message Passing]]

Processes have separate address spaces on purpose: one process cannot scribble on another's
memory, which is most of what memory protection buys you. IPC is the controlled way back
through that wall, and there are exactly two ways to build it.

| | [[Shared Memory]] | [[Message Passing]] |
|---|---|---|
| Idea | map one region into both address spaces | kernel copies data from sender to receiver |
| Speed | fast; ordinary loads and stores after setup | slower; a [[System Call]] and two copies per message |
| Who synchronizes | **you**, with [[Semaphores]] and [[Locks]] | the kernel, for free |
| Failure mode | races, corrupted shared state | full buffers, blocked senders |
| Across machines | no | yes, this is what sockets are |
| Kernel involved | only at setup | on every message |

**The trade is one sentence: shared memory is faster and hands you the
[[Critical Section Problem]]; message passing is slower and takes the problem away.**

## The concrete mechanisms

Everything in Unix is one of the two:

- [[Piping]] and named pipes ([[FIFO]]): message passing, one-way byte streams.
- Message queues and sockets: message passing, with structure.
- `shmget` / `mmap` shared regions: shared memory.
- Signals: message passing, degenerate case, one bit of message.

Between [[Thread|threads]] of one process none of this is needed, because they already
share an address space; see [[Process Communication]].
